messages.author: 28f7cf43544f2467
messages.subject: Legend Question
parts:
I ran into an issue today that I would like to know if it is a R bug,
ggplot2 bug, or (most likely) just plain R ignorance on my part.

I am experimenting with stacked bar plots and noticed an issue with
the legend. When I plot an unfiltered data set (t1) with all factors
("tasks") shown...I get the following plot (http://
ggplot2.googlegroups.com/web/AllFactors.jpg).

When I subset the data into a new data frame (t2) and plot a
restricted list of only a few of the original factors...the legend
seems to still display all factors from the original data set even
though none are in the newly subsetted(?) data frame (http://
ggplot2.googlegroups.com/web/SubsetFactors.jpg).

Is there a better way to do this?

t1 = data frame
ggplot(t1,aes(day,fill=task)) + geom_bar() results in (http://
ggplot2.googlegroups.com/web/AllFactors.jpg)

t2 = subset(t1,t1$robot==robottype)
ggplot(t2,aes(day,fill=task)) + geom_bar() results in (http://
ggplot2.googlegroups.com/web/SubsetFactors.jpg)

messages.subject: Re: Legend Question
parts:
Hi Nick,
Take a look at the structure of the factor after the subset, and
notice that empty levels are not dropped. You can get rid of the empty
levels by factor() -ing the factor again.

-Ista

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Legend Question
parts:
On Fri, Feb 26, 2010 at 1:05 AM, Nick S <n.si...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks for the reply.
>
> What does seem to remove the extra factors from being plotted in the
> legend is the following:
>
> ggplot(t2,aes(day,fill=as.character(task))) + geom_barplot()
>
> Any idea why this would ignore the extra factors left over from the
> original...un-subsetted data frame?
>

After subsetting your factor had some levels which were not present in
the data anymore. By converting the values to a character vector, only
the levels present in the data are used:


f = factor(letters[1:5])
s = f[ f %in% letters[1:3]]

levels(s) # all the levels are still present
levels(factor(s)) # updated factor levels
s[ , drop=TRUE] # alternative

as.character(s) # the values are converted

HTH,

baptiste

huh, I must be missing something, because I seem to be able to control the order of facets using levels in factor:

testd <- data.frame(
question = c("QuestionA","QuestionB","QuestionC"),
student = c("Student1","Student1","Student1","Student2","Student2","Student2","Student3","Student3","Student3"),
answer = c(40,120,170,10,100,175,20,150,190)
)

# controling y axis order using limits
# note that documentation doesn't describe this (in fact says only 2 values allowed in vector)
# http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_discrete.html
# "limits: numeric vector of length 2, giving the extent of the scale"
# although later on that page the example shows this form, but still only
# using two.
ggplot(testd,aes(y=question,x=answer)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~student,ncol=1) + scale_y_discrete(limits=c("QuestionB","QuestionC","QuestionA"))

# Using a factor to control order of facets:
testd$studentF <- factor(testd$student, levels=c("Student2","Student1","Student3"))

ggplot(testd,aes(y=question,x=answer)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~studentF,ncol=1)
# works with facet_grid too...
ggplot(testd,aes(y=question,x=answer)) + geom_point() + facet_grid(.~studentF)
ggplot(testd,aes(y=question,x=answer)) + geom_point() + facet_grid(studentF~.)
